A volunteer at the UK National Archives discovered a rare 1776 Exeter printing of the US Declaration of Independence, celebrated as an incredible historical find.

A volunteer cataloging Royal Navy letters at Kew discovered one of only 11 surviving Exeter printings of the Declaration of Independence, taken from a captured American privateer in 1776.

The Bright Side:
An officer's ancient failure to submit all seized papers to the court preserved a priceless document that might have otherwise been lost to history.

There is no modern deception here. The minor historical discrepancy lies in the WHO (the captain's withholding of papers) versus the WHAT (the legal capture process).

The captain chose to bypass formal court transparency to share the document directly with naval superiors. This historical shortcut ultimately preserved the artifact for centuries.

The Unavoidable Truth: The rare document is authentic and safely archived.

The Unavoidable Lie: The capture papers were fully processed by the maritime court.

The archival trail is clear. While Captain Fitzherbert's crew swore a false oath to the prize court, the physical preservation of the document remains an absolute fact.
